text: An activity defines an action. A linked service defines a target data store or compute. An integration runtime is the actual compute infrastructure that bridges the two — every single activity you've built across this entire course has genuinely been running on one, whether you noticed it or not.

Four real capabilities come from this one piece of infrastructure. Data Flow, executing mapping data flows in managed Azure compute. Data movement, copying data across stores. Activity dispatch, routing transform activities out to external compute like Databricks. And SSIS package execution, natively, in managed Azure compute.

Notice something genuinely important here: a data factory's own metadata — its pipelines, its trigger history — lives in one fixed region, set back when you created it. An integration runtime's location is completely independent of that. You can create one in a specific region purely to keep data movement inside that region for compliance reasons.

Three real types, three real jobs. Azure IR is fully managed and serverless, for cloud-to-cloud data movement, activity dispatch, and data flows. Self-hosted IR is software you install yourself, bridging to on-premises or private-network data. And Azure-SSIS IR is a managed cluster of Azure VMs, purpose-built to run existing SSIS packages natively.

When more than one IR could genuinely apply to an activity, Data Factory resolves it with a clear precedence: self-hosted always wins over an Azure IR in a managed virtual network, which in turn wins over the global, autoresolve Azure IR. Next: Azure Integration Runtime — the default, serverless runtime behind nearly everything you've built so far in this course.
